To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
CPE is a multifunctional, cytotoxic protein that disrupts the paracellular permeability of intestinal epithelia by damaging TJs.
CPE kills mammalian cells via two different cytotoxic pathways and that CPE disrupts TJs by binding occludin.
CPE is a cytotoxic toxin that damages tight junctions and may induce inflammation, all of which contribute to the enteric pathogenicity of CPE-producing C. perfringens isolates.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the cytotoxic mechanisms and pathogenicity of CPE.
the elucidation of the molecular basis of CPE cytotoxic and TJ-damaging activities.
the mechanisms of CPE action, and we hope to use that knowledge to design new approaches to control C. perfringens food poisoning.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the enterotoxin is a unique, multi-functional toxin with cytotoxic and TJ-damaging activities.
CPE is a multifunctional toxin, which is able to induce cytotoxic, TJ damage and proinflammatory effects.
CPE is a multifunctional protein with cytotoxic, paracellular barrier-damaging and (possibly) proinflammatory effects.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
we now understand the basic mechanisms involved in the cytotoxic and TJ-damaging activities of CPE.
CPE is the most complex and best studied bacterial enterotoxin.
CPE has a complex, multifunctional, and dynamic mode of action.
The main takeaway from our work is that
CPE is a complex toxin that kills mammalian cells by a number of mechanisms.
CPE is not a simple pore-forming toxin, and its cytotoxicity is more complex than previously believed.

CPE is a complex, multi-functional protein with a variety of activities, and that it is important to understand all of those activities in order to develop an effective treatment for patients with CPE-induced GI disease.
